items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created to improve the Rails Internationalization docs.

Detail

A big change is that I've reordered the guide to start off with beginner friendly content, then move into managing locales in requests (as its own section for easier navigation), then API features and finally an advaced section.

Other parts tackled from here:

  • Remove the Contributing section which references a inactive forum.
  • Remove the authors section, as we don't mention the authors in other guides.
  • Unlike other guides the introduction does a quick summation of steps to take to implement I18n. The whole introduction should probably be rewritten with a "After reading this guide, you will know..."
  • "This means, that in the :en locale, the key hello will map to the Hello world string. " This could probably be replaced with a code example:
    I18n.t('hello')
    => "Hello world"
  • Code examples would also improve the mentioned ActiveModel validation messages.
  • "Managing the Locale across Requests" should probably be a top section.
  • - The first example of setting the locale through a param is missing a header. Something like: "Setting the Locale from a request parameter"
  • - In the "Passing Variables to Translations" section the product_price switches from $ to € which is probably not typical. Maybe a better example would be using "dutch" and "spanish" where dutch uses "€ 100" and spanish "100 €".
  • - The note about number_to_currency should probably be a NOTE instead.
  • - The line "(Future Rails versions may well bring this automagic localization to assets in public, etc.)" can probably be removed, as I don't think this has been implemented or is planned.
  • [ ]
  • - The returned values for the examples in "Basic Lookup, Scopes, and Nested Keys" would make things clearer.
  • - The resulting HTML for "app/views/home/index.html.erb " in "Using Safe HTML Translations" is missing. This would help in seeing what gets escaped and what doesn't.
  • - The example usage in "Translations for Active Record Models" like User.model_name.human are probably clearer in a code block.
  • - The methods mentioned in "Overview of Other Built-In Methods that Provide I18n Support" would be clearer with code examples.
  • - The "Custom Translations" examples are more clear if we also show the output:
  • I18n.t "date.formats.short" # => "%b %d"
  • [ ]
  • - The "Using Different Backends" section shows an example how to add a different backend, but doesn't go into detail on how to use that backend.
  • - The "Using Different Exception Handlers" also mentions how to configure Rails to handle MissingTranslationData exceptions. That section should probably be renamed "Handling Missing Translations" or "Handling I18n Exceptions". This section could probably use an example as well:
  • > I18n.t('missing')
  • Translation missing: en.missing (I18n::MissingTranslationData)
  • and maybe examples can be added for the other exceptions as well?
  • - The "Translating Model Content" section should not link to 3rd party gems. This section should probably just be a note in the introduction instead.
  • [ ]

Additional information

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Follow up to #56855

This Pull Request has been created because this restores parity between insert_all and create for all value types, while preserving the performance gain for the common case.

Detail

PR #56855 added a fast path in InsertAll::Builder#values_list that skips type.cast(value) when the column type is serialized. The rationale is sound for Hash/Array input: Mutable#cast is deserialize(serialize(value)), which for a serialized column means coder.load(coder.dump(value)) — an expensive round-trip that produces the same Ruby object back, so calling it before SerializeCastValue.serialize is redundant.

However the optimisation is incorrect when value is already a String. In that case the call chain is:

 SerializeCastValue.serialize(type, "already_encoded")
 # => type.serialize("already_encoded")
 # => coder.dump("already_encoded")   # encodes *again*
 # => double-encoded garbage in the DB

With create the path is:

 type.cast("already_encoded")
 # => coder.load(coder.dump("already_encoded"))  # round-trip normalises it
 # then type.serialize(normalised_value)
 # => coder.dump(normalised_value)               # correct single encoding

The fix is minimal: only skip cast when the incoming value is not already a String. Non-String values (Hash, Array, custom objects) are the ones that benefit from the optimization and are safe to skip. String values must still go through cast to match create behavior.

Mutable#cast is deserialize(serialize(value)). For Type::Serialized, serialize calls coder.dump(value) and deserialize calls coder.load(...). So cast("already_encoded_string") → coder.load(coder.dump("already_encoded_string")) — which is the right normalization behaviour matching create. It skips this entirely for serialized types, so a String value bypasses cast and goes straight to SerializeCastValue.serialize(type, value) → type.serialize(value) → coder.dump(value) — one encoding on top of the already-encoded string.

The Mutable#cast round-trip is only redundant when the value is already the canonical Ruby-domain object the coder expects to receive (Hash, Array, custom class). A String is ambiguous — it could be a raw Ruby String object being stored, or it could be a pre-encoded database representation — and only running cast disambiguates it the same way create does. The check is cheap (is_a? is O(1)) and only activates the full path when actually needed.

Four test cases are covered, all using topics.content (a text column with serialize). ReverseCoder is deliberately non-idempotent: dump("foo") → "encoded:foo", so a second dump on that would produce "encoded:encoded:foo", which is immediately visible as corruption in the assertion.

Additional information

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created because Rails is missing a way to insert arbitrary load hooks for specific autoloadable classes. Zeitwerk has support for this with on_load("MyClassName"), but Rails doesn't provide a public-api-friendly way of accessing the Zeitwerk loader in Rails (the only way is Rails.autoloaders.main, which is private API). Even if you were to use this API, the semantics here are slightly different to ActiveSupport.on_load.

Detail

This Pull Request adds ActiveSupport.on_module_load to fill this gap. Instead of using to_prepare to eagerly load a class:

Rails.configuration.to_prepare do
  MyClassName.config = true
end

We can now instead do something like this:

ActiveSupport.on_module_load(:MyClassName) do
  self.config = true
end

Additional information

More information here: #57224

items.content_html:
This pull request uses NOT ENFORCED in disable_referential_integrity on PostgreSQL 18.4+ as a follow up pull request for
Since this pull request depends on #57377 then created as a draft one.

Motivation / Background

Detail

  • On PostgreSQL 18.4+, disable_referential_integrity uses NOT ENFORCED/ENFORCED instead of DISABLE TRIGGER ALL/ENABLE TRIGGER ALL, requiring only table ownership rather than superuser privileges. check_all_foreign_keys_valid! skips NOT ENFORCED constraints since VALIDATE CONSTRAINT cannot be applied to them.

  • Within Rails, disable_referential_integrity is called by insert_fixtures_set (which already wraps the call in a transaction) and by truncate_tables. The toggle and restore here are also wrapped in a single transaction to protect public API callers that invoke disable_referential_integrity outside an outer transaction.

  • Without the wrap, if a foreign-key restoration fails (e.g., a row inserted in the block violates the constraint), the initial NOT ENFORCED toggle has already been committed, leaving originally-ENFORCED constraints in a NOT ENFORCED state that is indistinguishable from intentionally-NOT-ENFORCED ones on subsequent calls.

  • NOT ENFORCED also suppresses referential actions (ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT). This achieves the same goal as the reverted #27636

Additional information

Refer to #57377 how NOT ENFORCED / ENFORCED works.

items.content_html:
This pull request adds enforced: option for foreign keys on PostgreSQL 18.4+

Motivation / Background

On PostgreSQL 17 or earlier, bypassing foreign key checks requires DISABLE TRIGGER ALL, which needs superuser privileges. Re-enabling triggers does not re-validate existing rows — so invalid data can silently slip in.

PostgreSQL 18 introduces the NOT ENFORCED option for foreign keys, which fixes both: the table owner can toggle it (no superuser needed), and switching back to ENFORCED re-validates all rows. A remaining blocker — that toggling lost the DEFERRABLE / INITIALLY DEFERRED attributes Rails relies on — was fixed in PostgreSQL 18.4, so Active Record can finally support this.

A follow-up pull request will update disable_referential_integrity to use NOT ENFORCED on PostgreSQL 18.4+.

Detail

  • NOT ENFORCED foreign keys are available since PostgreSQL 18.0, but DEFERRABLE was lost on them until 18.4 ("Fix loss of deferrability of foreign-key triggers", https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/18.4/). Rails therefore requires PostgreSQL 18.4 or later for this feature.

  • When enforced: false is passed to add_foreign_key, the constraint is created as NOT ENFORCED, meaning PostgreSQL skips referential integrity checks during DML. PostgreSQL marks NOT ENFORCED constraints as NOT VALID internally (and VALIDATE CONSTRAINT does not apply to them), so the schema dumper outputs both enforced: false and validate: false.

  • change_foreign_key toggles the enforced status of an existing foreign key. Without this method, users would need to issue raw ALTER TABLE ... ALTER CONSTRAINT SQL to disable enforcement temporarily (e.g., for bulk DML that loads the referenced and referencing tables in arbitrary order) and then re-enable it.

Additional information

  • PostgreSQL 18.0 Release Notes

Allow CHECK and foreign key constraints to be specified as NOT ENFORCED (Amul Sul) § §

  • PostgreSQL 18.4 Release Notes

Fix loss of deferrability of foreign-key triggers (Yasuo Honda) §

  • A previous attempt to avoid the superuser requirement via SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED was reverted because referential actions other than NO ACTION cannot be deferred, even when the constraint is declared DEFERRABLE.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

number_to_phone leaves a stray fragment at the front when a multi-character :delimiter is used with a number that has no area code:

number_to_phone(5551234, delimiter: " - ")
# => "- 555 - 1234"   (expected: "555 - 1234")

number_to_phone(5551234, delimiter: ", ")
# => " 555, 1234"     (expected: "555, 1234")

The :delimiter option accepts any string with no documented length restriction, but convert_without_area_code stripped the leading delimiter (produced when the first capture group \d{0,3} is empty) with slice!(0, 1) — assuming it would always be a single character.

The bug only fires when the first capture group is empty (≤ 7 digits and no :area_code), so 10-digit US numbers and single-character delimiters never trigger it. It has been dormant since the line was introduced in #3314 (2011): the test suite only exercised single-character delimiters (where slice!(0, 1) is coincidentally correct) or 10-digit numbers (where the first group is non-empty so no leading delimiter is produced).

Detail

Strip delimiter.length characters instead of a hard-coded 1:

number.slice!(0, delimiter.length) if start_with_delimiter?(number)

start_with_delimiter? already guarantees delimiter.present?, so the length is at least 1. String#slice! is character-based, so multibyte delimiters are handled correctly too:

number_to_phone(5551234, delimiter: " - ")  # => "555 - 1234"
number_to_phone(5551234, delimiter: "—")    # => "555—1234"

Single-character delimiters, 10-digit numbers, :area_code, :country_code, :extension, and empty-delimiter cases are unaffected (verified — full number_helper_test.rb is green: 22 runs, 819 assertions, 0 failures).

Additional information

Tests added for ASCII multi-character and multibyte delimiters, and a CHANGELOG entry is included since this is a user-visible behavior change.

Checklist

  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If the default commit message added by GitHub when amending the PR title and description is used it might result in a poor commit message.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

ActiveRecord::TestCase#check_connection_leaks scans each pool during teardown to catch connections left owned by background threads.

ConnectionPool::Reaper can legitimately hold a connection under reaper_lock while it performs maintenance. The leak check currently inspects pool.connections without taking that lock, so teardown can race the reaper, report a leaked connection owned by AR Pool Reaper, and kill the maintenance thread even though no test leaked anything.

Detail

Synchronize the leak scan with pool.reaper_lock so teardown waits for any in-flight maintenance to finish before classifying in-use connections as leaks.

Add a regression test that reproduces the false positive by holding a connection for maintenance from a thread named AR Pool Reaper. The new test fails against origin/main and passes with this patch.

Additional information

This surfaced as an unrelated CI failure while validating #57367, where the reported leaked owner was the pool reaper thread.

Tests

  • cd activerecord && ARCONN=postgresql bundle exec ruby -Itest test/cases/test_case_test.rb -v
  • cd activerecord && ARCONN=postgresql bundle exec ruby -Itest test/cases/reaper_test.rb
  • cd activerecord && ARCONN=postgresql bundle exec ruby -Itest test/cases/associations/has_and_belongs_to_many_associations_test.rb
  • bundle exec rubocop activerecord/test/cases/test_case.rb activerecord/test/cases/test_case_test.rb
items.title: Prevent false leaked-connection reports during reaper maintenance

items.content_html:
Calling to_i on very long strings can take a very long time and could be used as a DoS vector. Users should validate input lengths before calling to_i, but we can do it somewhat automatically in ActiveModel.

This commit limits auto-integer coercion to strings that are <= 1kb. For example, if we have a model like this:

ActiveRecord::Base.connection.create_table :users do |t|
  t.integer :age, limit: 1
  t.timestamps
end

class User < ActiveRecord::Base; end

puts User.create(age: '9'*5_000_000).age

Before this commit, age would return a very large number and also take a long time to convert to an integer. After this commit, age returns nil.

At first, I based this change off the width of the column from the database, but that doesn't work because ActiveRecord supports "auto integerization" of slugs. So for example you might have a controller that looks like this:

Post.where(id: params[:id]).first

We expect slugs to come in with values like "123-hello-world-etc", so limiting based on column width doesn't work. I just picked 1024 out of the air, we could make this a configuration option, or increase the number.
items.title: Limit the size of strings we call `to_i` on in ActiveRecord

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Rails registers its internal development welcome route from routes_reloader.run_after_load_paths.

That hook currently calls app.routes.append on each route reload. RouteSet#append stores append blocks persistently, while route reloads clear and finalize the realized routes. As a result, repeated reload_routes! calls in development add another internal GET / welcome route each time.

Detail

Register the internal welcome route append block only once per application boot, while preserving the existing append behavior and route ordering. This keeps app-appended root routes taking precedence over the internal welcome route.

Additional information

No existing issue found for this specific duplicate welcome-route behavior.

Tests

  • ruby -c railties/lib/rails/application/finisher.rb
  • ruby -c railties/test/application/routing_test.rb
  • bundle exec rubocop railties/lib/rails/application/finisher.rb railties/test/application/routing_test.rb
  • cd railties && bin/test test/application/routing_test.rb -i '/not duplicated|appended root/'
  • cd railties && bin/test test/application/routing_test.rb
items.title: Prevent development welcome route from duplicating on route reload

items.content_html:
Summary

Also support dynamic store: option in rate_limit like we already do for some of the other params.

Motivation / Background

The rate_limit API supports method names and callables for some of the parameters.
Extending this to :store allows applications to resolve the cache store at runtime (per-request, per-tenant, gradual cache migrations, etc.) without boilerplate conditionals in controllers. Static usages untouched.

Detail

Changes ActionController::RateLimiting so that store: accepts:

  • Static values (unchanged behavior), e.g. store: RedisCacheStore.new(...).
  • Instance method names (symbols), evaluated in the controller context via send (like we already do for to and within).
  • Callables (lambdas/procs), evaluated in the controller context via instance_exec following the existing pattern.

Resolution logic:

  • If value is a Symbol → send(value)
  • Else if it responds to call → instance_exec(&value)
  • Else → use as-is

Additional information

  • Aligns with earlier changes to allow method names for :to, :within, :by, and :with.
  • Negligible overhead (a couple of conditional checks) on the rate-limited path.

items.content_html:
When create_or_find_by rescues a RecordNotUnique inside a transaction, the previous where(attributes).lock.find_by!(attributes) applied the attributes twice — and if the relation already had conflicting scope conditions for the same key, the generated SQL would be contradictory (e.g. WHERE nick = 'irvan' AND nick = 'bob'), raising RecordNotFound.

Fix by using rewhere(attributes).lock.take! instead: rewhere replaces existing conditions for those attribute keys rather than stacking them, and take! fetches the record without adding further WHERE clauses.

Fixes #57192

Motivation / Background

create_or_find_by raises RecordNotFound when called on a scoped relation
inside a transaction. When rescuing RecordNotUnique, the previous code used
where(attributes).lock.find_by!(attributes), which applied the lookup
attributes twice on top of the existing scope. If the scope already had a
condition for the same key with a different value, the SQL became contradictory:

-- Subscriber.where(nick: "irvan").create_or_find_by(nick: "bob") inside a transaction
WHERE nick = 'irvan' AND nick = 'bob' AND nick = 'bob'

This always returns zero rows, raising RecordNotFound instead of the existing record.

Detail

Replaced where(attributes).lock.find_by!(attributes) with
rewhere(attributes).lock.take! in the transactional rescue branch of both
create_or_find_by and create_or_find_by!.

rewhere removes any existing scope conditions for the specified attribute
keys before applying the new ones, preventing conflicting duplicates.
take! then fetches the first matching record without appending further
WHERE clauses.

Checklist

  • This Pull Request is related to one change.
  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. Fixes #57192
  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
  • CHANGELOG updated in activerecord.
items.title: Fix create_or_find_by duplicating WHERE conditions on retry within transaction

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This Pull Request has been created in response to the comments by @byroot here and here.

Detail

This Pull Request changes allows adding custom date formats to to_fs without modifying the global Time::DATE_FORMATS or Date::DATE_FORMATS hashes. Custom formats are added via ActiveSupport::TimeFormats.register or ActiveSupport::DateFormats.register, and will only be available to Time#to_fs, and Date#to_fs respectively.

At the same time, the existing Time::DATE_FORMATS and Date::DATE_FORMATS constants are still supported for backward compatibility, but they are now deprecated and will be removed in the next version of Rails. This encourages users to migrate to the new approach for better encapsulation and to avoid potential conflicts with other libraries that may also modify the global date formats.

ActiveSupport::TimeFormats.register(:month_and_year, '%B %Y')
ActiveSupport::DateFormats.register(:short_ordinal, ->(date) { date.strftime("%B #{date.day.ordinalize}") })

Time.now.to_fs(:month_and_year) # => "February 2024"
Date.today.to_fs(:short_ordinal)  # => "February 21st"

Additional information

The ActiveSupport::TimeFormats.list and ActiveSupport::DateFormats.list are initialized to Time::DATE_FORMATS and Date::DATE_FORMATS respectively, and not frozen, so that appending to the constants can still modify the lists until the constants are removed completely. This is important for backward compatibility.

However, as soon as a call to the respective register method is made, the list is modified and frozen considering that the user has opted in to the new API.

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

This PR has been created because I'd like a safer way of running a deep value transformation on ActionController::Parameters. Today, the only option is params.to_unsafe_h.deep_transform_values { ... }, which discards the permitted/unpermitted distinction and returns a plain Hash. This forces application code to bypass the strong-parameters guardrails for a routine normalization task (e.g., stripping whitespace from every nested string before validation).

ActionController::Parameters already exposes deep_transform_keys and deep_transform_keys!, and Active Support already extends Hash with deep_transform_values. This PR completes the symmetry by adding
deep_transform_values and deep_transform_values! to Parameters, matching Hash#deep_transform_values while keeping the result inside ActionController::Parameters with permitted? preserved.

Details

params = ActionController::Parameters.new(
  user: {
    email: "  ALICE@EXAMPLE.COM  ",
    profile: { bio: "  Hello world  " }
  }
)

params.deep_transform_values { |v| v.is_a?(String) ? v.strip.downcase : v }
# => #<ActionController::Parameters {"user"=>#<ActionController::Parameters {"email"=>"alice@example.com", "profile"=>#<ActionController::Parameters {"bio"=>"hello world"} permitted: false>} permitted: false>} permitted: false>

# The bang variant mutates in place
params.deep_transform_values! { |v| v.is_a?(String) ? v.strip : v }

# permitted? status is carried over
params.permit!
params.deep_transform_values { |v| v }.permitted? # => true
items.title: Add ActionController::Parameters#deep_transform_values

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

When using multiple databases you traditionally can't join across databases but SQLite has the unique ability to include different SQLite databases in the connection and treat them one big database.

Take this setup for example:

class ApplicationRecord < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.abstract_class = true
end

class Course < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :entrants
end

class OtherRecord < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.abstract_class = true

  connects_to database: { writing: :other }
end

class Entrant < OtherRecord
  belongs_to :course
end
default: &default
  adapter: sqlite3

development:
  primary:
    <<: *default
    database: storage/dev.sqlite3
  other:
    <<: *default
    migrations_paths: db/other_migrate
    database: storage/other_dev.sqlite3

Prior to this patch if you were to execute Entrant.joins(:course).where(courses: { name: "Ruby Development" }), a StatementInvalid error will be raised because Entrant and Course live in different databases. But if you execute ATTACH DATABASE 'storage/other_dev.sqlite3' as other, you bring entrants into scope and can join over to it. This patch prepends the database name to those external database table calls to avoid conflicts.

Given that we know where these models live, database wise, and SQLite offers us the an avenue to join across databases, we should automatically include those databases into scope and extract that away from the developer when executing a query.

Since SQLite can be write constrained, if you have a particularly write heavy table, this would allow you to move the table to it's own database and free up the primary database for more writes while still allowing you to treat it as if it was in the primary database.

Motivation / Background

Fixes #57334.

The SendGrid ingress already returns 422 Unprocessable Content when the optional envelope parameter contains invalid JSON. However, if envelope is valid JSON with a malformed shape, the controller calls envelope["to"].each and raises NoMethodError.

Detail

This Pull Request validates the parsed SendGrid envelope before using its to recipients. Malformed envelope JSON now follows the existing unprocessable response path and no inbound email is created.
